utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, is the Defence ready to cross-examine Ms. Hanson?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't -- I don't think even Mr. Hannis knew that examination-in-chief had finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understood that the Court was going to consider my request for some additional time. I have reviewed the list, Your Honour. There are four documents remaining that were not part of her report that were for presentation only. I think I could do that in 15 minutes or less, and I would request an opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you're allowed to spend 15 minutes on --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- further examination-in-chief. Yes, Madam Usher. Would you escort Ms. Hanson to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's happening, may I simply inquire when Your Honours would propose to deal with the outstanding reports back on housekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I intend to do that later this day, but as you may have noticed, sometimes I take the last minutes before the break rather than the first minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, may I say of course we're entirely in Your Honour's hands how that happens but there is a problem about taking the last minutes before the break which is, since we don't know exactly how long it will take Your Honour, we run into that difficulty. With the greatest respect, Your Honour, it may be that taking the very beginning of a break is -- just from a practical point of view has some advantage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it has some advantages. It has some disadvantages, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, if Your Honour is talking about time constraints, Your Honour, we assure Your Honour that we have nothing to do on that except to report and deal with it as briskly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Hanson. May I first of all remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. The examination-in-chief will continue for another 15 minutes. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Hanson. When we left off on Friday there were still some matters I had not been able to ask you about. In the interest of time, I'm just going to talk about the four remaining documents that were presentation only as the others are either footnotes or otherwise mentioned in your report. With that, the first one I'd like to go to is presentation tab 315, and it's master tab number 439. This is from a 26 May minutes of the joint meeting of the TO battalion command and the Kalinovik command. Could you tell us why you put this in your presentation folder.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we see from the documents that I have footnoted, the -- the Trnovo Crisis Staff set up the TO and coordinated closely with the command of the TO. Here we see a joint meeting of the battalion command and the military post Kalinovik. We note that Colonel Bundalo and Lieutenant Jovovic division commander were present, and they state that all four -- in the middle of the page, both in B/C/S and the original: "All forces in Trnovo will be returned under the command of Kalinovik. So Kalinovik take all forces in Trnovo should the situation deteriorate." So coordination between the TO and local military there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next one I wanted to show you is master tab 442, which is presentation tab 316, and these are minutes from a meeting of the Trnovo Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm all right with this one, but I'm just inviting Mr. Hannis just to go a tiny bit slowly on this for this reason: That the master tab reference -- I was intending to work this morning from my computer on these matters where I have this material, but the numbering has changed. The -- and also the master tab numbers or the master tab numbers just given don't appear at all because the numbers run out before we get there, and the presentation tab numbers have changed, something I've mentioned to Mr. Hannis. I think I've got this one which is minutes from SDS Trnovo Crisis Staff which used to be 318 and is now 316. Is it -- may I simply inquire through Your Honours. The translation reference is L0017057, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm just pointing out that the translation that I'm working on is ET 02276221.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 316. Yes, thank you very much. I think I see that. Well, I hope I do. Document related to mobilisation of conscripts and addressed to Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Minutes of the meeting of the SDS Crisis Staff, 27 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I have an extra hard copy of the three documents I'm going to show I can hand to Mr. Stewart for his use this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That would be much appreciated, Your Honour. Your Honour sees the difficulties with this numbering. Thank you. I'm grateful, Mr. Hannis, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Hanson, if you could tell us what you wanted to bring to our attention in this document?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, the close ties between the Crisis Staff and the TO command and the involvement of the Crisis Staff in the preparations for military actions, the first line Radivoje, the president of the Crisis Staff, tells Danilo to make a list of command personnel and "let us verify it one of these mornings." Danilo Goljanin, you will recall, was chief of the TO command staff. I find it significant that the Crisis Staff here is seeking to verify the command personnel. At the bottom of the -- towards the bottom of the first page in the B/C/S, third -- second speech by Radivoje in the English translation, at the end he says: "We can or, rather, we must establish contact with the army in Lukavica and Kalinovik." Again, contact with the army. On the next page in the B/C/S, still on the first page in the English, Danilo says -- yes, it's towards the bottom of the B/C/S, 02276222, the speech by Danilo. He reports discussion at the command last night, and he says: "As concerns the defence of Trnovo, Bundalo completely agrees with the concept except that the forces for taking the village should be stronger." So reporting conversation with Bundalo about plans for what he terms the defence, but -- of Trnovo but the defence includes forces for taking over the village. And lastly at the very bottom of the English page and on the next page in the B/C/S, just wait to go see -- yes. Speech by Radivoje in the lower half of 02276223. Radivoje says: "We will hold all meetings together from now on." I take this to be with the TO command. So close coordination and preparations for military actions including taking over the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next one I want to show you, now we go to another municipality in your Rajlovac case study, presentation tab number 319. It's master tab number 13. This is from minutes of a meeting of the Bratunac SDS Municipal Board in October of 1991. Can you tell us about this one?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I noted in my report, Bratunac is an exception to the pattern of Crisis Staffs first being established after the 19 December instructions, that is at the end of December. In Bratunac, the minutes of the Municipal Board show that the SDS Municipal Board formed a Crisis Staff in late October 1991. However, this Crisis Staff follows the pattern of being formed on the orders of the SDS leadership. I would note in the agenda item 2 is implementation of tasks and conclusions reached by the Serbian Assembly of BiH, and number 3, appointment of a -- of the Crisis Staff in Bratunac municipality with the purpose of implementing protective measures for the Serbian people. Under item 1 in the minutes the president told the board about the founding of the Serbia Assembly, its tasks and aims. The board unanimously accepted all the tasks. And item 3, a Crisis Staff is formed. In my report a similar document when the information first came to Bratunac at this time, the Crisis Staff is -- the meeting is held and the tasks assigned explicitly, it says, on the order of Karadzic. Here he is also conveying the information from the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, may I ask you, you said on item 2 it is implementation of tasks and conclusions reached by Serbian Assembly. I read agenda item 2, "election and appointment of the Crisis Staff," or am I wrong? Or am I on the wrong document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is 02 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that I'm in the wrong document. I am in 319 now. I should be in 319 now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's where I am, 319.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are two similar meetings, one of a smaller. The first meet something a smaller of what he calls the Presidency of the Municipal Board which says much the same information. And then a few days later this is the meeting of the larger Municipal Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With similar agenda. That's what I was referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you have any explanation for how it is that a Crisis Staff was formed in Bratunac in October of 1991 when we didn't see Variant A and Variant B instructions until December?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do see at this time that Karadzic declares a state of emergency in the SDS, and there are many references to municipal boards receiving and implementing his reports for a state of emergency. Bratunac is the only one that, as I say, forms a Crisis Staff but it does so explicitly -- explicitly ties it to instructions from Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally the last one I want to show you is presentation tab 325, Your Honours, master tab number 432, and this is from a February 1993 meeting of the SDS Municipal Board.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In February -- on February 1, 1993, it was the first session of the Municipal Board since the outbreak of the war, and Mr. Deronjic gives a perspective of the outbreak of the conflict. I find significant here his statement -- this is on the right-hand side of -- in the B/C/S of 02192726, in which he says: "The Main Board of the SDS and the local boards were the only bearers of activity for preparation and organisation of Serbian people and giving resistance to the enemy." So noting again that the role of the SDS in organising the Serbian people. In fact he says they were so good at military organisation -- says at the bottom of the English first page -- in the middle of the B/C/S page: "It was estimated that the situation today would have been much better and all the military goals might have been achieved if the command of the Operative Group Drina of the former JNA did not interfere." So in the general context of this speech he's saying how well they had organised and prepared for war and perhaps he says could have done even better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, two other matters. One is I think when I introduced presentation tab 319 I gave the wrong master tab reference for that. It should be 431 is the master tab number. And finally, Your Honour, earlier in my presentation we had two documents in which Ms. Hanson had indicated we believe that it was Mr. Krajisnik's signature on. Those were the appointments of some republican War Commissioners. I believe the documents were presentation tab 75 and 76. And we had inquired what the Defence position was on that. I wanted to bring that up again before I've left the matter. And with that I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Is that -- that is Mr. Krajisnik's signature on both those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an additional question to put to the witness regarding your report, Witness. Do you have it in front of you? Do you have your report in front of you? I would like us to go back to page -- yes. I'd like us to have a look at page 14 of your report regarding the role of the Crisis Staffs. Number 35, paragraph 35. If I understand you correctly, what you're saying is the Crisis Staff was there to ensure coordination between the police, the army, and what you call the paramilitaries, and we are talking about coordination between these organisations and the political party. Am I understand you correctly -- do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And I would also add -- yes, the party and also the government, that is, the municipal structures and the Bosnian government organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I mistaken in thinking that within the Crisis Staffs there were commissioners, in other words, representatives, people who were entitled to talk on behalf of these institutions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Crisis Staffs as opposed to War Presidencies, I have not seen any indication of their commissioners. In Djeric's instructions of the 26th of April, 1992, he does say that commissioners will be appointed. But I do not see in documents of Crisis Staffs anybody named as commissioner. We saw in the discussion in November 1992 in the Assembly the significance given to deputies. They said whether it's a deputy from the Assembly or a commissioner isn't important, but I do not -- although I see Assembly deputies as members of Crisis Staffs, I do not see them referred to as commissioners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the War Presidencies, there were commissioners within the War Presidencies, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what is stated in the presentational decision of 31 May 1992. I'm checking my memory, but I do not recall seeing anybody as a commissioner on something that we know of that is identified itself as a War Presidency. It seems that in that sense, the presidential decision on War Commissioners, which superseded the decision on the formation of War Presidencies, was -- was intended to form War Commissions where the role of the commissioner was clarified. We know there were commissioners before the formation of -- before that decision on War Commissions, but we do not see them, their presence or activity reflected in minutes of Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 38 of your report you same the problem: [In English] "Krajisnik in his role as a member of the Presidency responsible for the work of -- of the republican commissioners." [Interpretation] That's where I do not really understand. Would you be able to clarify that sentence for me, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We know from the minutes of the Presidency of 6 July 1992 that Krajisnik was named as the member of Presidency responsible for the work of commissioners. We know from his speech in the Assembly in November 1992 that he says he was very well-informed about the work of all the commissioners. So I see that his identification as the member of the Presidency responsible for the work of commissioners he had that task that no one assigned to him that until then seems to have been perhaps genuine -- generally shared among the Presidency, but he was given that as an explicit task. And as he said in his speech, it worked well. He knew what they were doing. He knew that they did their work well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me go a bit further. When you write "responsible for the work of the republican commissioners," what do you mean? What do you mean exactly? What does it mean? Because for me it means that he was responsible for the actions of the commissioners. Therefore, he was due to follow and supervise their work. What did you understand from the -- from reading the documents you studied about that matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of those minutes and the other documents I've seen, responsible in the sense of he was the member of the Presidency to which commissioners would turn first. Of course it's important to understand that not everything that happened strictly according to the normative documents. Informal relations played a great role, and it could well happen that someone in the municipal organ might have turned to Karadzic or somebody else first out of -- from knowing him or from formal lines, but within the Presidency as they were dividing up their tasks, Krajisnik is the one who is to deal with and to know about commissioners. I do not understand it to mean responsible in the sense of any -- bearing the consequences of their actions necessarily more than any other member of the Presidency, but the point of contact is how I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. President Hannis, no further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I would only note for Judge Hanoteau that we have a witness coming next week who will talk more about commissioners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to cross-examine Ms. Hanson?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, you will be cross-examined by Mr. Stewart, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, the -- between 1990 and 1992, and according to your CV, you were engaged in research in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the -- what was the precise period in terms of month to month?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in August 1990. I believe my work didn't really start until September, and I left in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was your research into specific fields?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was research for my dissertation work. I was at the time a graduate student at Yale University in modern Balkan history. The topic of my dissertation was the army of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in the period between the First and Second World Wars, and the bulk of my research in Belgrade I did at the archives of the Military Historical Institute of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And your curriculum vitae of course gives your various study periods and your work appointments. There was not a list appended of publications. Do you have publications?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have two translations that I made that -- one in a book and one in a journal, but no original writings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And those particular translations, are they in any particular way germane to the issues with which -- on which you're giving evidence to this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: One is not. The other would be. It is -- it was a translation of some statements or one statement, I honestly can't recall at this moment, that appeared in the book called "Why Bosnia" edited by -- I'm sorry, I forget the name of the editor. It's in the library and I can obtain a copy of that book. It was published during -- I think in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was the particular topic there?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was statement of a Bosnian Muslim who had survived an execution in Karakaj in Zvornik, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There might -- there were other statements as well. I'm sorry. That's just when they were. It was a collection of statements of Bosnian Muslims regarding the conflict. It was -- but it was only translation, I repeat. It was a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It sounds as if they were specific, related to a specific incidents?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was nothing general. It was experience of ordinary people in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Ms. Hanson, you are -- is it right to say you were in effect the team leader for the purpose of preparing this report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not the team leader. I -- in the LRT that would be Pat Treanor, but this report is -- in writing this report, I received the help of my colleagues mostly in terms of having documents brought to my attention because other people in the team would know that I'm working on Crisis Staffs, would show me documents they came across that they thought would be of interest. And the first section of the report on the other bodies I also received some -- I relied upon or looked at the work of colleagues who wrote about those. But I am the principal person on the team for the question of Crisis Staffs, municipal Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When I say "this report" I should make it clear. I'm talking about your report dated 13 July 2002 as slightly amended on the 26th of November, 2004.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's the shorthand of your report.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The LRT, is that legal research team? I --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Leadership research team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Leadership research team. And Mr. Treanor is the head of that team?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So from what you're saying in answer to my question about whether you were the team leader for these purposes, the position as you've described is this: That in fact the team leader for the purposes of this report, the one I've referred to, is Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is my team leader. I am a member of the LRT. I wrote this report. I don't know what you mean in for the purposes of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Hanson, it is this: I had put it to you that you were the team leader. You said, well, no. And your answer indicated that if so far as there was a team leader, which presumably there must be, it was Mr. Treanor. So let me take if from there. Was Mr. Treanor involved in any way in the preparation of this report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like my other colleagues, he brought to my attention documents that he thought would be relevant, and as the leader of my assigned work group, the leadership research team, he reviews -- he reviewed this and all other documents that go out under our names. All -- all reports or memos are issued through Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the process is this, was it, Ms. Hanson, that your -- your final draft report went to Mr. Treanor? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to recall. The final draft, because it's not -- because this report in its final form was for the Court, I'm not sure that he would have had a final sign-off on this form. But in general, my written memos and reports he signs off. They go through him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I had -- Ms. Hanson I should make it clear and to the Trial Chamber I had deliberately and specifically avoided the phrase "signing off" in that question, because, Ms. Hanson, I was going to assume, and please confirm if this is correct, I was going to assume that the actual signing off of this report was done by you because it is your report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual signing off of this final form I would say was done by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That is why I avoided that phrase and therefore put it to you that before you signed off, the final draft of your report before signing off went to Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly don't recall whether -- because there is the final final, once all the footnotes are checked and double-checked, in the sense of that final final form, because it did not take the form of a memo which is -- goes through Mr. Treanor, I can't say for sure at what was the last stage at which he cast his eyes upon this. But certainly -- certainly he looked at -- looked at it right up until the end, but because this goes from me to the Court, I would not say that this final final version -- the version that goes to the Court goes through him. It has my name on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, forgive me. I think we've already so far as agreement is necessary, I think we've already agreed about that. At the point where you personally sign off your report, that is your report subject to the amendment in November, which is relatively minor. So I think we've agreed about that. The -- is it this, then, that possibly leaving aside footnotes that either the first version or something extremely close to the last version of the text on the body of your report went to Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if Mr. Treanor -- well, either he did have or if he had had any suggestion or proposals or questions, then he either did or would have raised them with you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you, without exploring into any detail, did you have debate and discussion with Mr. Treanor in the course of preparing your report about the text of your report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What were -- expressly and explicitly, what were your instructions for the preparation of this report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My instructions were to write a report on the municipal Crisis Staffs of the Bosnian Serbs, on their functions, on their role in the state and their actions in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were those instructions given to you in writing?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When were they given to you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to reconstruct when I was assigned to the -- the team dealing with this area. When I was assigned to this team, I was told in general terms that my work would involve Crisis Staffs and I was to look into the issues that I named, and as the work evolved it became -- it gradually took on the form of an actual report, but it started just as a research. And it was in the spring, and I'm -- I'm -- can't recall if it was the spring of 2000 or 2001 right now, I'm sorry. I can check my -- my work and tell you when I started, but I can't remember. It was actually -- now I can reconstruct. It was 2001. Sometime in the spring of 2001, Mr. Treanor told me I would now be working on the team, Bosnian Serb team, and that I was to look into Crisis Staffs. As I said, it evolved towards this report but I was not originally told, "Write a report for the Court."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is this the -- is this the only report which you have signed off on for a Trial Chamber in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the only full research report. For the Milosevic case I had written a much shorter memo of I believe about eight pages on a fairly restricted question, the question of the Supreme Defence Council, and I signed a declaration regarding that report. So I believe it did enter the Milosevic case in that way, but I did not appear in court, and I don't know to put the fate of that memo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you were given your instructions for the preparation of this report, who gave them to you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did he -- do you recall? Did he give them to you at a face-to-face meeting between you and him?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you make a note of the instructions he was giving you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When did you subsequently make a note?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I made notes as I began researching, but I did not make a note of any assignment as such. As I said, it was told in general terms find out about Crisis Staffs, but it was in such general terms as to where I should start researching. There were no specific -- nothing more specific than what I said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So is it -- is it a process under which the -- your terms of reference evolved as you were doing the work?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [French interpretation on English channel].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because I now receive French on channel 4. Perhaps I speak a few more words. I do not hear any more French so I take it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is that a takeover by the French language, Your Honour, or is it in addition to the other channel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it was -- if you would call it a takeover. It was French nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was teasing Judge Hanoteau, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would say the -- the assignment evolved as it went along.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. So would you -- would you then summarise, Ms. Hanson, what you -- what you would -- understood your instructions to be at the point where you signed off the report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that time, it -- it was -- I understood my assignment to be to explain to the Court the functioning of Bosnian Serb Crisis Staffs, their role in the state and the powers they had. To -- at first I would say it was not necessarily clear at the beginning that this would get to the Court. It was for all of us to understand Crisis Staffs. By the time the report was signed off, it was clearly intended to play a role in the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At what point did it become clear that there was to be a report for the purposes of the case against Mr. Krajisnik and Ms. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot now recall the point in time at which -- I would say the evolution came as it became clear that there was enough good material to write a substantive report and as -- there was enough there to answer. There was enough to be said, and the Prosecution team felt that this was, as I understood them, this was something that needed to be addressed in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So is this what happened: There was an express request from the Prosecution team to produce a report with a view to giving evidence in the case against Mr. Krajisnik and Ms. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would say the request evolved. First the Prosecution team wanted to know about Crisis Staffs, and then on the basis of my report, they then asked for the -- they then felt the report could also -- could be used for court and should be. I should write a report or continue to work on it, expand my report to that end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's clear, your department, you are a -- there's no mystery about it. You are a resource for the Prosecution, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We are part of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But -- so, Ms. Hanson, it's clear, isn't it, that beyond the slightly general description that you've given of your instructions and the nature of the report, the evolution involved or reached the point at which your report was to be specifically directed towards the case against Mr. Krajisnik and Ms. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reached a point at which it would in itself as a report play a role in the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it plays a role in the case, Ms. Hanson, because you are here and your report is before the Trial Chamber. But more specifically, at the risk of repeating my question to you, the report was to be specifically directed towards the case against Mr. Krajisnik and Ms. Plavsic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report was -- when I -- knowing that I was writing a report for court is different than writing, as we all do in the LRT, shorter memos specifically responding to Prosecution requests about specific kinds of evidence. This was intended to explicate Crisis Staffs for the benefit of the Prosecution but also for the benefit of the wider court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, what do you mean, Ms. Hanson, when you say "for the benefit of the wider court"?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that I'm here -- I also write smaller, as I said, or carry out smaller research assignments that assist the Prosecution, retrieving various kinds of evidence, analysing documents, but they don't all reach the level of this, of getting to court. They answer smaller questions as well. And knowing that this was -- this was for the Court, I would say I knew when I was writing it in this version that it was not just for the Prosecution. It was to provide everyone with an understanding of Crisis Staffs, not to argue the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's -- I put it to you, Ms. Hanson, the -- your job and your task is entirely consistent with your assisting the Prosecution and with your -- of course in accordance with the solemn declaration you give assisting the Trial Chamber to your honest best. That's -- both of those bits are true, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, it's a little -- I suggest a little disingenuous to suggest, for example, that you're here to help and benefit the Defence. You're not suggesting that surely, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the form of the question. That's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it stems -- I'm sorry. It stems directly from what the witness herself has said. It was to provide everyone with an understanding of Crisis Staffs, and everyone includes the Defence. So my question is trying to obtain a proper explication of that witness's answer specifically given in this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say everyone includes the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it does as a matter of -- if you assert it in those terms, of course it does, Your Honour. And what I'm putting to the witness is precisely what I did put, that it's a -- I don't mean in the least -- in the least bit offensively, Ms. Hanson, and please don't take it that way, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please specify. If you say here to help and benefit the Defence, I take it to help and benefit the Defence in understanding the functioning of the Crisis Staffs or in any other way to help the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm suggesting, Your Honour, that what I'm putting to the witness is this: That when Ms. Hanson says that it was to provide everyone with an understanding of the Crisis Staffs not to argue the Prosecution's case, I was putting to Ms. Hanson that the idea of course it may enhance everybody's understanding somewhere that the idea that Ms. Hanson, that part of the purpose was to help the Defence's understanding of the position. That's just unreal.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm here to present the documents which cast light upon those issues of the Crisis Staff. I would hope that the more information would help everyone. I'm not saying that I'm -- I'm not here to argue anybody's case. I'm presenting the documents as I understand them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, if we -- if we the Defence had asked to sit down and interview you and go through your report with you, you would hardly have agreed, would you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that calls for speculation on her part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. I withdraw the question then if that's too speculative. Let's focus -- I don't really want to pursue this particular specific line any more with respect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's get back to this. It's described as research report prepared for the case of Krajisnik and Plavsic. Ms. Hanson, at some point instructions were either given to you, weren't they, or it's clearly understood by you that part of the purpose of this report was to explore and present links and actions and involvement of Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Krajisnik in relation to Crisis Staffs. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And apart from any general exploration and research into Crisis Staffs and apart from any research which would apply to anybody with any involvement, you have included -- and that was part of the purpose of the report, you have included matters where you believe you have found those specific links between Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Krajisnik and the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What -- not document by document, of course, there are hundreds of footnotes anyway, Ms. Hanson, but by in first place description of categories and sources, could you please summarise the sources of the material on which you prepared your report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: For some Crisis Staffs we have minutes of meetings. Some of these are very extensive collections. So I looked at minutes of Crisis Staffs. I looked at other documents we have from Crisis Staffs to Crisis Staffs about Crisis Staffs such as municipal Official Gazettes where we have those, minutes of the -- minutes of the government, minutes of the Presidency, Assembly minutes, intercepted conversations, then larger collections of documents that were from -- from municipalities about municipalities, and then a great many documents from the RS government archives. And as I said, other documents were brought to my attention by other people, so I would look at those and then relate it -- documents related to those. So various kinds of collections, various kinds of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If the first place, Ms. Hanson, and -- [B/C/S on English channel].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I suppose it was about time the English language got its comeuppance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question. I was listening to it in B/C/S but I'd prefer to hear it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I will do my best in my language, Ms. Hanson. I was asking you in the first place if you could give some estimate of the total amount, total number of documents which were examined for the purpose of preparation of your report.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number would be in the thousands, but I couldn't say anything more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Tens or hundreds?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tens. Less -- ballpark figure, between 110.000 [sic] actual pages, I would say, of some -- some -- you know, in reviewing a collection I might glance at a document and say it's no use and move on, and in that sense I would say it was thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the transcript doesn't help you or anybody for the moment there because it's come across as between 110.000 actual pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Between 1.000 and 10.000?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been saying thousands. It's certainly more than a thousand. So when I say thousands, I mean a couple thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, we must see vastly in excess of a thousand pages just in the presentation binders let alone the master binders, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think it's clear when we're talking about pages or documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you're referring -- when you told us between 1 and 10.000, were you taking about pages or about documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I do accept that correction, Your Honour. I have elided documents and pages. So.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I ask just to clarify that, and I see Ms. Hanson is thinking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest, Your Honour, I wasn't counting. I would say documents, but some documents are one page, some are more. I didn't read many documents of hundreds of pages. So I would -- this is -- I'm not trying to be evasive, I simply don't tell you in any more precise terms, but I would say it was in the thousands, both of pages and pretty much that as of documents since many documents are one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I'm not suggesting you're being evasive about it and of course my not distinguishing documents and pages didn't help. I acknowledge that. Can we just try and quickly approach it a different way. Can you form a rough estimate of the ratio between the material which is actually presented -- is given to the Court in the master binders and the material you looked at which has not found its way into master binders? Just as best as you can do.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say maybe roughly 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 10 per cent what?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the documents that I looked at and read as useful in some way, not counting the ones I simply looked at and said irrelevant. But I would say maybe 1 in 10 of documents that I read got here. Again, that's a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, that's helpful. Thank you. The -- well, the Trial Chamber will decide whether they find it helpful. It's the answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I seek a clarification. If you say 1 in 10 of documents that I read got here, do you mean in the material presented to us or in your thinking? You understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I would say of -- of the documents that I actually read and got some information from, that I found relevant, that contributed to my understanding of the Crisis Staffs, I would say roughly 1 in 10 of those was cited in my report or in my presentation. That's a very rough impression I have sitting here, because for one municipality I might have dozen -- hundreds of pages, and another municipality I might have many fewer. So the -- the proportion wouldn't be the same all over. And some documents will say the same thing in different ways. But of documents that contributed to my understanding of the Crisis Staffs, as an order of magnitude I would say about 1 in 10 was cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's just a little bit -- I'd slightly avoided all, withdrawn the verb presented because of the distinction between presentation binders and master binders, so I had -- I had understood you to be saying that when you say documents that got here, I'd understood that as meaning the master binders. His Honour explored the matter further. If it's 10 per cent which has contributed to your thinking and been used, then of course it follows that the total is even more than if the 10 per cent is what's in the master binders, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, then, the -- when you say -- when you refer to material that -- that you have looked at, and of course I want to make it clear it's totally understood that some pieces of paper just get turned over and put on one side, we all do that, but when you say that you have done that, for these purposes that includes any members of the team to whom you've delegated that task, does it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not delegate tasks as such to other members of my team. Other members of my team would review document collections and come across documents for their own purposes, which they would then bring to my attention, and I would look at those documents and others related to it, but I would not -- did not tell members of my team, Go and find this for me. Tell me about this or that. It was more they would -- they would bring specific documents or collections that they thought would be relevant to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So when you had material for your own perusal, you would peruse it yourself rather than pass it down the chain?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was that because you felt that that was what, that the only confident, reliable way of doing it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was writing the report so I would look at the documents relevant to my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What -- again it has to be -- well, I don't know whether it has to be fairly rough. That rather depends on the record-keeping, Ms. Hanson. What -- what would you assess or what can you tell the Trial Chamber is the total number of hours that you've spent writing this report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I received the assignment in the spring of 2001, and the report was finalised a year later. I did not work only on that report in that year. I had many other taskings. But this was my largest research project in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Does that mean that you spent more than half your time on it during that year?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than half, yes. I would -- I can't recall everything I did that year, but that seems a fair assessment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And can we take it that at least some significant part of the rest of your time when you were -- all your time was spent on Crisis Staffs in the broadest sense during that period, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I would answer questions on all kinds of -- kinds of topics. Crisis Staffs was my main research, as I said, but I still had other obligations as a member of the leadership research team and would answer other kinds of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would a fair summary be then that you say more than half your time during that period was spent on this report? Would it be a fair suggestion, then, that more than half of the rest of your time was spent on Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I meant that more than half of my time was spent on Crisis Staffs. Crisis Staffs and report as -- I see as the same thing, the -- this ongoing research that evolved -- this ongoing research into Crisis Staffs that evolved into that report. That I would say would take up more than half my time, but there were other matters on which I conducted research.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How many people were -- how many people were involved in the writing of this report that work here in your department?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote the report. The first few paragraphs I did rely on material written by one colleague for another report, but I looked at the documents involved and reached the same conclusions. There were four or five other people in my section, as I said, to whom -- who would bring documents to my attention, who would help me in my understanding of some issues, but I -- I wrote the report. So you say involved in the writing of the report. I work in a team but I talked to other people. But in terms of the selection of -- pardon me. The selection of documents and the conclusions reached, it is my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. The report that you mention, the report of one of your colleagues, you said you relied upon the material written by one colleague for another report, is that a publicly available report in the sense that it has been presented to --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believes it was presented in the ARK case, Brdjanin case. There was another report by Mr. Treanor, a report by Mr. Treanor in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it's Mr. Treanor you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm just asking you to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The passage involved was -- the paragraphs were written by another colleague, Andrew Corin, on the background. The -- the -- if I could just refer to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I think it would be helpful if you could just give an idea --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The legal origins --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- of which passages. You're not talking about the executive summary. You're talking about the next section, the legal origins.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Paragraphs 5 through 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, paragraphs 5 through 8. That report was like -- was similar to Mr. Treanor's report in this -- in this case, and I -- I looked at -- I used the research of a colleague in that passage, but as I said I looked at the documents and reached the same conclusion. I didn't just cut and paste and never look at the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the very last sentence, then, at paragraph 8 in your report -- well, in fact one can -- or take the whole sentence. I'm really particularly focusing on the bit from the semicolon. But the whole sentence, five, six lines up: "The Crisis Staffs were entrusted by the party to operate on their own initiative in accordance with the policies and positions of the SDS until they were able to ensure the conditions for the municipal organs of the new Bosnian state to function; however, they were themselves in accordance with the policies and positions of the SDS responsible to a considerable extent for the creation of the crisis conditions and the collapse of the regular organs of municipal government." Was that sentence or any significant part of that sentence drawn from that other report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was my sentence. I'm -- the part that I meant the -- was relying on the colleague's work was the more -- the legislature involved in the other paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The legal stuff?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's not your field, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I could have written it, but because the work had been done by a colleague, I didn't do it. But the legal stuff in terms of I can look at a municipal statute or a constitution as well, and I did for other aspects of my work. I'm simply saying I didn't bother to repeat the research of that -- of those paragraphs because it had been done. As I said, I looked at his sources. I could have written those paragraphs, but I'm acknowledging that the original work had been done by someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did -- just because anybody in -- any of the team that contributed to this work on your report claim any firsthand knowledge of any of the relevant events in, let's say, 1990, 1991, 1992 in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe one member of the team was in Bosnia at some point during the war, but I'm not sure whether he was there as early as 1992. He worked for a different organisation. So in that sense he has some firsthand knowledge, but as I say, I don't think he was there as early as 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Does it follow therefore from the way you just put that that this particular colleague didn't give you or didn't purport to give you for the purpose of the writing of your report the benefit of any firsthand knowledge which he might have had from Bosnia during that period?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. He did not give me any such firsthand knowledge for -- for the writing of this -- for any of the -- anything relating to this report. He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is the -- is your report, therefore, based entirely on -- well, I'll make it clear as a preface, Ms. Hanson. I'm going to ask you whether it's based entirely on documents. Now, of course you've got something in your brain when you start to read the documents, so let's take that as a given, but so far as sources and information for the purposes of this report is concerned, is it based entirely on research into documents?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents as understood in the larger sense of intercepted telephone conversations as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, yes, of course I --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- will acknowledge and --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document is based on the documents in that sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- and I think you've already indicated in evidence, but perhaps confirm that you have not yourself been engaged in a study of the broader context except so far as directly necessary for the purpose of writing this report.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean by the broader context --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I will give you an example. When you were asked about membership and dates of the expanded Presidency, you -- you disclaimed knowledge of that because that sort of issue you regarded, is this fair, as -- well, for others, if you like, but not a necessary part of your work for these purposes?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- it is not a part of this report. It is certainly a question that I could be expected to answer in the course of my daily work as a member of the leadership research team in my office with all my notes and sources available, but in -- here in the courtroom talking about Crisis Staffs, I did not want -- couldn't speak with any confidence at that moment about it. It's something that I could easily answer, as I say, in my office with my other sources, but it's not my area of expertise that I could speak with total confidence in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we take it, Ms. Hanson, when we explore your report, which I promise you we are going to do very soon, can we take it that there is no significant supporting documentation for the propositions in your report beyond what you draw attention to in the footnotes or -- and/or have referred to specifically in your evidence already to this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many documents which support specific conclusions. I made a selection for the footnote. For each footnote I would make a selection of what I thought were the best examples, the most clear and concise examples. There are many other documents which support in a general way what I say but not in a way that can be usefully referenced to a particular page or sentence or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, with that you've actually answered my next question, so we got two for the price of one, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that does actually conclude -- unless I can think of anything wonderful over the break which Your Honours might be about to take. That concludes that chapter, if you like, of my cross-examination. So I would move on -- if this is a convenient point for the break, I would move on to the substance of the report immediately after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think this would be a good moment then for the break rather than to start for the next five minutes with your next subject. So we will adjourn until ten minutes to 11.00, and the Chamber is looking forward to your wonderful thoughts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, may we -- you've got a copy of your report in front of you, I take it. May we look, please, at paragraph 20. In the second sentence you say that: "Municipal Crisis Staffs received orders from and reported to the SDS leadership via the Main Board, the Bosnian Serb Assembly, or personal approaches to Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik and others." Now, we can -- so we can break that up, can't we, into category 1 received orders, and category 2 -- received orders from -- and category 2, reported to. That would be -- do you agree that would be a reason way of breaking down your proposition there?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can say -- you can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was advising you of your agreement, but that is how I'm going to do it. So, Ms. Hanson, let's take -- let's take orders, then, first. Crisis Staff received orders from the SDS leadership via various organs and people. You -- your footnote 24 here -- or your footnote is number 24, and you give your examples of orders from the SDS central organs. And, Ms. Hanson, can we take it that consistently with the approach which you had indicated immediately before the break, you have looked for the clearest and best - was your word - examples to illustrate the points in the body of your report, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So may we look, then, at the first item, and the way I'm doing it, Ms. Hanson, is so far as possible to take the presentation binders, it may be occasionally that we're thrown onto the main binders, but that document , it's the first footnote on page 9, SDS, the 19th December, 1991, instructions; letter by secretary of Executive Committee. And that's presentation binder 2, tab 61. Now, I just want to be clear how physically we're going to handle this because you don't have the presentation binders in front of you, do you, Ms. Hanson?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have them yet. May I clarify something?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a semicolon, so that I take as the first example the 19 December instructions, and then the letter by the secretary of the Executive Committee is another item.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like they were run together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. The instructions themselves?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We will come to those, but specifically the letter --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- by secretary of Executive Committee. And that's at presentation binder 2, number 61, tab 61. If at any time, Ms. Hanson, you see immediately or if at any time it's not the right document, I'm sure since it's your report you will inform the Trial Chamber and, please, me straight away. But this is the letter that's referred to in the footnote, isn't it, letter by secretary of Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Agreed?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So as -- this is in -- in its essentials, this is, if you like, a high-level notification to the Crisis Staffs that they are going to be replaced by War Commissions.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is a letter to the presidents of three of the -- governments of three of the Serb autonomous regions that Crisis Staffs are going to be replaced. It's the same information, but it's a question of to whom it's addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, if I've got it clear what you're saying, you're saying yes you agree with the proposition I put to you with -- put to you that this is a notification that Crisis Staffs are going to be replaced by War Commissions. We agreed on that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it's not two Crisis Staffs. That's how I took --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's take it in stages, Ms. Hanson. You were agreed on that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right? Where you're differing with the way I put it is that you're saying that it isn't in fact notification to the Crisis Staffs but it's addressed as somebody else?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Addressed to the commissioners, people who are going to be commissioners for the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the only difference is that as a support for your proposition in the text that municipal Crisis Staffs received orders, in this particular instance the particular example which you have put in the footnote here is not a direct receipt of orders by municipal Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is directed to the War Commissioners who are to work in the War Presidencies. So as members of that body, it's directions to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And well as notification of that change to the addressees, of course, of this particular document, they are being told that they should continue as War Commissioners to perform the duties set out in Article 4 of the decision.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that's it. I mean, it didn't -- in essence, this particular document says no more than those two things, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are other things to be read from this document, but -- relevant to this issue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I put to you one can't really read -- although there are some details of days, one can't read into this document any more as any sort of information or instruction than the two points that War Commissions are going to replace Crisis Staffs and that the duties are to -- to be to carry on performance of those set out in Article 4 of the decision. Really --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I simply -- I use this document for slightly other information, but relevant to what you're talking about here, yes, that is correct what it says there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. And the next items you refer to in the footnote, SAOs, 24 February 1992 decisions. And this is a batch of items, isn't it, that follows -- that follow in the next -- the next few sections? We can look at 2, 63, tab 63. Is that -- is that one of those items or not?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not presentation tab 63 that I see. I believe those decisions were not in my presentation. So they'd be in the master binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is this the master binder available? Could that be available to you, number 2. Yes, I think this is in fact an example of somewhere where we have to switch to the master binder, not the presentation binder. So that -- my apologies, that reference would there. So if you go to tab 62 in the master binder. Do you have that, Ms. Hanson?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we've found it. The binder's a little awkward.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So 62 is dated 24 February, SDS Executive Board at its 8th Session held on 6 February adopted the following, and the decision was that Mr. Lukic, though we actually -- we all seem to be perfectly confident that that's a typo or miswriting and that it should be the same person, Rajko Djukic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which is mentioned on the bottom. It's a coincidence that he's the person there. The -- it's -- it's a notification of his appointments with a summary of his tasks; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then 2, 63 is a very similar document, isn't it, relating to of course a different person and a different SAO?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, 63. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 64 doesn't really seem to be different from 63. Perhaps is there some explanation?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 63 I have the appointment of Radoslav Vukic, and on tab 64, Vojo Krunic, and Radomir Neskovic. So it's a series of decisions. Essentially the same decision but different names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, what's happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be I'm the unlucky one here. What has happened is that I have the Vukic appointment twice in different tabs in a slightly different form and I don't have the document that you've just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But it doesn't matter, perhaps, because, Ms. Hanson, even blind on that particular point I'm simply inviting your confirmation that what is at 64 is essentially -- it's the same type of document. It's the same type of notification. It's the same type of appointment simply relating to different people and a different place?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've put on the ELMO the original because I see the translation is the same -- is a translation of another document but the original can show you its different names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then -- so the translation's the problem. There is a flaw in the bundle as far as the translation is concerned?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like me to read the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps for the record if you -- not the whole thing I suggest, Ms. Hanson, but perhaps if you just read those key introductory sentences so that it is on the record as to what it is.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the only difference -- the sentence that is different from the others is: "[Interpretation] The members of the Executive Committee of the SDS of the BiH, Mr. Vojo Krunic, and Mr. Radomir Neskovic, shall be designated as members, coordinators entrusted with coordination for SAO Eastern Herzegovina." [In English] So another difference is to which SAO they're appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's 60 -- or 65 is a similar document that relates to Mr. Sarac and Mr. Djukic. The SAO or the SAO as I've learned this morning is called in the business, Romanija?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then 66. Again, would you prefer -- it's a corresponding document relating to Mr. Jovanovic and Mr. Prijic, and they've been slightly differently phrased in the English anyway. They were appointed coordinators of the city -- it's not phrased differently. Coordinators of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Similar corresponding document; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the last one in this batch at binder 67 relates to Mr. Mihic and Mr. Babic, Mr. Slobodan Babic for the Northern Bosnia SAO or SAO?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what we've got -- what we've got so far in your footnote, just a checklist, what we've got so far as your examples of orders are the 19th December, 1991 instructions themselves?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which we haven't dwelt on for the moment. The notification on the 31st of May, 1992, from the Executive Committee of the SDS that Crisis Staffs are to be replaced by War Commissions, and that their duties are to be Article 4 and so on, and then these -- this batch of appointments of particular gentlemen in relation to particular places to this designated role of coordinator?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that they are -- one of their jobs is to involve themselves in the work of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But -- well, Ms. Hanson, --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is in the decisions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Ms. Hanson, would you probably agree if they weren't going to do that there wouldn't be much value in their appointment at all, would there?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what else -- there's indication of other jobs they did, but I would just note that their job was -- one of the tasks assigned was to be involved in the work of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Ms. Hanson, that's the -- that's the sum total of what you have been able to present to the Trial Chamber as orders received from the SDS leadership to municipal Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also presented what I thought were relevant excerpts from Assembly sessions and intercepted phone conversations in the presentation, but those were not in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. We'll come to -- we'll come to Assembly sessions, then, but as far as -- and the other matter you mentioned, but so far as identified orders sent, in some way addressed, in some way finding their way into the hands of municipal Crisis Staffs directly or indirectly, this is the sum total of what we see as orders from the SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So do you agree not one of those relates to any specific action to be taken by anybody in relation to the work of any Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The 19 December instructions have steps to explicate what the Crisis Staffs are to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let me make that clearer then. The 19 -- 19 December instructions as you present them are a -- they're a general order applicable to all the Crisis Staffs intended to be established in accordance with those instructions.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The documents that we've just looked at involve appointments, a reference to duties in general terms rather than in relation to any specific contemplated action. Agreed?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And they include, of course, notification of the specific appointments that are mentioned in those documents. Agreed?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: None of them gives any order to any specific municipal Crisis Staff to perform any specific action. Agreed?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of those documents at this time, yes, that I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So we -- do we see anywhere here, leaving aside what you say about the December 1991 instructions, but let's leave those aside for the moment, do we see any order from the Main Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Leaving aside the 19 December instructions, which are apparently issued by the Main Board, no. Of the other documents that we have looked at here, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And as far as these documents are concerned, we clearly don't see any, or do we, from the Bosnian Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of these documents, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And we don't see any order coming from there Karadzic personally or Mr. Krajisnik in any of these documents we've just looked at, do we?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these documents we have looked at, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So just -- although we won't explore that right now, but so far as the Bosnian Serb Assembly is concerned, your position is this, Ms. Hanson, is it, that such orders as came from the Bosnian Serb Assembly we can and must read in the minutes of those Assembly sessions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it correct, Ms. Hanson, that there is no written order that you have been able to identify given to any municipal Crisis Staff by Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No written orders, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. Let's -- let's look, then. That's orders, because I said I would divide it up into orders and reports. So let's now consider reports. The -- and you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
