And you correctly refer to the division of tasks recorded as adopted. And we see among other things, for example, Dr. Plavsic. We've touched on that previously in this case, her particular responsibilities. And then UNPROFOR as well. And then questions related to commissioners and the economy, Momcilo Krajisnik. And Ms. Hanson, you'd agree, wouldn't you, that that isn't intended as compendious? Those are two distinct areas of responsibility, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it's one, commissioners; and two, the economy.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my interpretation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik then, according to this agenda, then, this item, then he has been allocated on the face of this document that responsibility from the 6th of July, 1992, onwards; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But it follows, doesn't it, from your previous answers that there's not the slightest indication of his having had any specific responsibility for that task, the republican commissioner's task, before the 6th of July?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his speech in the Assembly in November 1992, Mr. Krajisnik says he was well-informed about all the commissioners and what they achieved. I take that to be some indication that -- well, he says he knew about all of them. Some of those may have been appointed before July. I would have to check the records on the exact appointments of the people he names, but he in his speech does not draw a distinction of the time before he was responsible and after.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well -- so apart from that, for what it's worth, which is no doubt for argument for another day rather than further cross-examination, apart from that speech that you refer to, there's not the slightest indication of Mr. Krajisnik having had any specific responsibility for republican commissioners before the 6th of July?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not more than any other member of the Presidency, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your report, though, based on this item 4 of the agenda, you are identifying him as the member of the Presidency responsible for the work of the republican commissioners but implicitly from that day the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that date he is the member.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And not before.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before, as -- not the one member before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have you seen any material which indicates any performance -- leave aside the speech in the Assembly that you mentioned a moment ago, okay? Apart from that, have you seen any material which indicates a discharge or attempted discharge by Mr. Krajisnik of that responsibility allocated to him under item 4?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before, I think his signatures on the appointments of two commissioners is an indication of his discharge of those duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we come to those then specifically, so again, all right, putting those on one side as well. So we've got two items in our shopping basket not to be bought; the Assembly speech and those two signatures. So putting those on one side, is there any material you have seen which indicates a discharge or attempted discharge by Mr. Krajisnik of that responsibility allocated to him under item 4 as from 6th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically regarding commissioners, no. Those are -- putting aside the evidence we've discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, then, if we go to the next footnoted items, that's footnote 52, and those are in the -- those may also be in the presentation binder, I'm afraid, but they're the next items in the master binder. They're 139 and 140. That's master binder 3, items 139 and 140. I'm fairly sure they're going to be found in the presentation binder somewhere as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's presentation tab 75 and 77.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's -- well, that will be most helpful to somebody. So it wouldn't make much difference to me right now, but thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And those are two -- those are the two items. Of course they're footnoted. That's what you're referring to when you say in paragraph 38 of your report: "In that capacity he apparently signed for Karadzic at least two Presidency documents dealing with the appointments of Commissioners." That's what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I have said earlier today I do confirm on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf that those are his signatures on those documents. What is the -- well, first of all, when you say he signed at least two Presidency documents, I'm not quarreling with the logic of "at least," Ms. Hanson, but is the position that that is the sum total of documents which you have seen signed by Mr. Krajisnik in a way which you would describe as being in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the only two documents dealing with republican commissioners which I have seen as -- identified as most likely signed by Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Those are signed by Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but until this morning I could only say most likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I understand. But so -- but you have seen no other documents which are or might reasonably be supposed to be signed by Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No documents regarding commissioners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's implicit. I'm sorry, that's implicit in my question, but I make that explicit. Yes?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, these are the only two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I believe His Honour Judge Hanoteau may have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hanson, I'd like to come back to what we said this morning. Do you have any indication as to the exact role played by these commissioners? And I would also like to know whether in any of these instances, namely the War Commissions, whether these commissioners had any hierarchical power and power over the way these organs operated, or were these commissioners the only links between the commission and political authorities or the army, the command in the army? And did these commissioners have in their capacity the right to give instructions to the commission itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, this is several things to answer. I hope I will address all your questions. The decision on the formation -- the presidential decision of 10 June on the formation of War Commissions specifies that the powers include -- or they have the -- they form the War Commission and can dissolve it. They name the members of the War Commission in the municipality and can dissolve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I don't know if it's helpful to have the document in front of you that refers to that. It's at tab 64 in the presentation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be glad if I could take a look at it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think that's the Presidency's. You want the War Commission's, which is tab 65 -- or 66. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 4, what I was saying, that the state commissioners form the War Commission - as I noted earlier, the translation is War Presidencies but we've confirmed that it's War Commission - and can dissolve them. To point out, to be quite precise, the second sentence he names the War Commission. In the third sentence he can dissolve the War Presidencies. It is "presidencies" in the original. He conveys directives issued by the War Presidency of the republic. That is in Article 3. To convey directives I see as he gets the directives from the Presidency, goes to the municipality and gives them to the municipal level. We also see in the Assembly discussion about the work of the War Commissions, that they convey the directives and -- to the municipal level and take information back up to the republican level. This is the most precise statement of the duties of the war -- republican commissioners. So that is what I base my description of their jobs, that with the evidence from the Assembly of how the commissioners described what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pardon. To get back to this particular point, we saw earlier on in the previous document that Dr. Koljevic said that he could not control -- he had no control over his commissioners, could not control the republican commissioners. Does this mean that he could -- or, rather, that the status of the person in charge of the commissioners had the power of control over them? Is that what it means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That -- that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this morning I understood he received the reports from the War Commissions. He analysed them, and he might have transmitted to them to whoever was entitled to read them. But here in the sentence of Dr. Koljevic, it seems more important that he actually have control over these War Commissioners on the way they worked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree. That does seem to be what Mr. Koljevic is saying. I -- it's the only indication I have of that sense of controlling. I do not see that elsewhere. I do not see it in the original descriptions. So I can't say more than what you have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart. Keeping in mind that we had a short list of matters on which the Chamber would like to receive brief reports, could you find a suitable moment to conclude for the day within the next one, two, or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly, Your Honour. If I may, I would simply like, while it's on the screen, and to follow up very quickly then:

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau's comment to you a moment ago, Ms. Hanson, where His Honour said, "This morning I understood he, that's Dr. Koljevic, received the reports from the War Commissions, he analysed them and he might have transmitted to them to whoever was entitled to read them." Ms. Hanson, the position is this, isn't it, that whatever his job was supposed to be, you don't point to any material which shows that he actually did receive reports from the War Commissions and analysed them and transmitted them, do you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I understood the judge's question to be what I meant in the sentence in my report when I said "responsible for," and I meant what we've been talking about, someone assigned in the Presidency to be, as it were, the point of contact for commissioners and that he was not responsible for the consequences of his actions. He was not -- I did not mean to say that I do not see him receiving such reports. That was -- I think the judge was saying his understanding of my response.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can leave cross-examination here conveniently, certainly for the moment, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, we have a few procedural issues to be discussed for a couple of minutes, but of course you're not required to be present. May I give you the same instructions as I did before: Not to speak with anyone about your testimony already given or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.00, in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we could back to what I had still on my list, that is P220. We are waiting for the confirmation by the Defence that it had to receive the document as it was sent on the 28th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Yes, and Your Honour, we confirm have no objection to P20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have D29 and D32. No, let me first -- P22 is then admitted into evidence. That should be the conclusion. Madam Registrar is looking at me as if I'm failing to keep control over the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's the kind of look Ms. Cmeric gives to me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's our fate, Mr. -- D29, D32, revised translations were provided by the Defence. OTP is about to report on whether there's any objections against these translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I'm not up to speed on that issue. I'll have to find out and get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then are you on any of the others? I'll tell you what they are. That's P -- no, P458, Mr. Stewart. That's for the Defence to report back if there were any further objections against P458 in its revised translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm feeling like goody-two-shoes so far. The answer is we have done our homework on that and we have no objection to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And P458 new translation replaces the old one and is admitted into evidence. Then, Mr. Hannis, P200/31. You're supposed to address the Defence objections by the end of the week. If you say, I'm not prepared, then at least you have it on your list for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and I understand that we're supposed to receive the revised translations today, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it says on my list, it says that due to an administrative error, OTP has not yet addressed the objections raised by the Defence in view of the translation. So you're expected to address any of the objections specifically in view of translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think we're expecting some material back from CLSS that addresses those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're still waiting. So "by the end of this week" was the end of last week, but I think it's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm informed we'll receive it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Then the next one is direction of the statement of Mr. Bjelobrk, whether the Defence would decide whether it had any further objections against the redacted statement of Mr. Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. What in fact, Your Honour -- I think the position was that we were going to report back to Your Honour on how much time we would need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with you. You are expected to report on how much time you would need to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There is a two-stage process with quite voluminous material. Stage number one involves Ms. Cmeric as the B/C/S speaker, and stage number two involves me as counsel. Your Honour, we haven't quite got to the end of stage 1. Your Honour, realistically given the other cause and key demands, I would ask Your Honour to -- I'm just trying to remember what day of the week we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're on the 7th today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 7th today. So it was the 4th. I actually ask Your Honour until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we say by the end of the week, if we make it this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't beginning to volunteer such a timetable, with respect, Your Honour. I really do need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean to give us an indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour. Yes, indeed. If it's the 7th today it's going to be the 11th, isn't it, on Friday. Your Honour, I was going to ask for two weeks after that but that actually does take us to the recess. So, Your Honour, may I have until the end of this session? It is -- I've spoken to Ms. Cmeric about it, Your Honour. It is going to require quite a bit of time. She anticipates it's going to take the whole day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When do we hear from you how much time that would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm asking for that time now, Your Honour. I'm saying -- I'm asking for that time until the recess. It's going to take a whole day according to Ms. Cmeric of my time, and that's not so easy to find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider. So you would like to have until the end of the recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not until the end of the recess, Your Honour. I am undertaking to do it before the recess. Yes, I believe that would be helpful if I were to have that material in before rather than after, and that is what I'm offering, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then I do understand that we hear from you then at the same moment about the exhibits in relation to Mr. Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It makes sense, Your Honour, with respect. If we can indicate specifically in relation to exhibits as an earlier separate item, we will do but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will let you know tomorrow if your request is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have, Mr. Hannis, the Defence was asking for -- I think for the audiotapes of D34 and D35, not specifically as an exhibit. These are the interviews, and you would inquire as to whether these tapes can be made available to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, that's one that I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from you when?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning. That's fine. Then the next item on my list says matters to be dealt with within two weeks, but that's not over yet, so we'll come back to that. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.
